extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians, geometry students, and correspondents to The Mathematician (mid-19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Derive and apply trigonometric relations (cotangent/cosecant identities) for three- and four-circle systems on a sphere in mutual contact, including formulas for circles through contact points, complementary circle-sets, special cases (internal contact treated as negative radii), and related loci and equilibrium conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. A — three mutually touching circles cot/cosec relation
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of the rectangles of the cotangents of the radii of three circles on a sphere in mutual contact is equal to the square of the cosecant of the radius of a circle passing through their points of contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given by considering triangle ABC with circle through contact points DEF and right-angled spherical triangles OD–lines, leading to equations sin^2 ρ cot p_i = cot(angle) and after multiplication/addition obtaining cosec^2 ρ = cot p1 cot p2 + cot p2 cot p3 + cot p3 cot p1. Two geometric cases (external contact and one circle touching internally) are treated explicitly, with algebraic sign changes for internal contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign convention for internal contact (negative radii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any property expressed for circles touching each other externally may be generalized to positions including internal contact by treating the radius of any circle touching the others internally as a negative quantity in the same expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows a single algebraic expression to cover all configurations; examples show substituting negative ρ for internally touched circles converts external-contact formulas into the correct internal-contact formulas (illustrated in derivations following Prop. A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of two circles through three contact points (spherical Soddy-like pairs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given three circles on a sphere in mutual contact there are two (distinct) circles which pass through their three pairwise contact points; the two radii satisfy a quadratic-type relation (two solutions corresponding to 'smaller' and 'larger' circles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from formula (8) (see other entries): the double sign corresponds to the lesser and greater of the two circles that can be described to touch the three given circles; sign convention handles internal touching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula relating cotangent of circle touching three given circles (general solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explicit relation gives cotangent of the radius ρ of a circle touching three given mutually contacting circles (radii r1,r2,r3); one form derived is 2 cot ρ = —cot r + cot r1 + cot r2 + cot r3 (with sign choices for smaller/greater solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equation (8) and variants supply the magnitude of the required circle; when one of the three given circles touches the required circle internally, take the corresponding radius negative. The upper/lower sign in double-sign formulas indicates smaller vs larger solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case formulas for three-circle contact (alternate algebraic forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: For configurations where one given circle touches the other two internally, alternate cotangent formulas are provided (e.g., cosec^2 ρ = cot p1 cot p2 − cot p1 cot p3 − cot p2 cot p3 in a derived case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text works through two geometric configurations (external contact, one internal) producing corresponding trigonometric identities; these exemplify how algebraic signs change with configuration and how to obtain the appropriate formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four mutually contacting circles: complementary-circle cot/sum relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If four circles with centres O0,O1,O2,O3 touch pairwise in six points, a complementary set of four circles may be drawn passing through those same contact points; the cotangents of radii of the two sets obey equalities, notably: (cot r0 + cot r1 + cot r2 + cot r3) = (cot p0 + cot p1 + cot p2 + cot p3) and likewise for sums of squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From pairwise equations (Prop. A applied to each triple), adding and rearranging yields identities (equations (3),(4),(11)) showing equality of the sum and sum of squares of cotangents between the two complementary quadruples. This is a spherical analogue/extension of circle-packing reciprocity (Soddy-like relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum-of-squares cosecant relation for four mutually contacting circles
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of the squares of the cosecants of the radii of four circles described on a sphere in mutual contact is equal to twice the sum of the rectangles of the cotangents of these radii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from equation (7): cosec^2 r0 + cosec^2 r1 + cosec^2 r2 + cosec^2 r3 = 2( cot r0 cot r1 + cot r1 cot r2 + ... ). The identity is presented as a neat property that follows from the earlier cot relations; students are invited to deduce further properties from equations (5,8,9,10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between the two Soddy-like solutions (Weddle's property)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ρ and R are the radii of the two circles which touch three mutually contacting circles of radii r1,r2,r3, then cot ρ + cot R = 2(cot r1 + cot r2 + cot r3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as Weddle's elegant result (equation (a)). It connects the two complementary solutions (smaller and larger circles) through a simple linear relation among cotangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special-case boundary conditions (centres on same great circle / tangent great circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Special-case reductions are given: e.g., if centres of three circles lie on the same great circle, certain simplifications occur; if the three given circles are touched by a great circle (a tangent great circle), then a specific form (e.g., cot ρ = cot r1 + cot r2 + 2/cot r3 -1 ) determines radii touching two circles and the tangent great circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists specialized reductions of the general formulas for these geometric constraints; these serve as practical formulas for boundary/configuration cases and for solving position as well as magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rutherford's relation — distances from a great circle/line for four contacting circles
rubrics_metrics.description: For four circles in mutual contact (on a sphere or in a plane), with one circle of radius ρ externally touched by the other three of radii r1,r2,r3, there is a relation linking the distances d and d' of the centres of two specified circles from the great circle/line joining two other centres to the sines of the radii (expressed separately for the sphere and the plane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement is given in parallel columns 'ON THE SPHERE. ON THE PLANE.' and supplies a means to relate geometric distances of centres to trigonometric functions of radii; use the spherical sine relations for spherical configurations, and the planar limit for plane cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beecroft's perpendicular-cosecant theorem for spherical triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of the squares of the cosecants of the perpendiculars from the angles of a spherical triangle upon the opposite sides is equal to one-fourth of the sum of the squares of the cosecants of the radii of the four circles touching the sides of the triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This links triangle-internal perpendicular lengths to the properties of the inscribed/tangent circle system; presented as a succinct geometric identity (useful for problems relating triangle geometry to tangent-circle configurations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lhuillier locus problem — straight-line locus via centroid construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Given m lines SA_i and a constant Q^2, the locus of point Y such that sum_i (SA_i * perpendicular from Y to line i) = Q^2 is a straight line. Specifically, the locus is a straight line parallel to the axis through the centroid Z of the given system; construct by finding Z, joining S to Z, taking a third proportional to SZ and Q, and drawing a line parallel to SZ at that distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The solution uses rectangular coordinates and centroid properties; Scholium 1 notes the more general case (lines not meeting at a point) still yields a straight line using analogous constants. The coordinate method is recommended as concise; construction steps are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of equilibrium for forces on four mutually contacting spheres
rubrics_metrics.description: For four spheres in mutual contact (three-and-three), the necessary conditions of equilibrium of forces acting at the contact points are: (1) the forces acting upon each sphere must have a resultant passing through its centre; (2) each resultant must lie in the same plane as the centres of the three adjacent spheres; (3) a specific relation (equation (a)) between the directions of the resultants must hold (a product-of-sines identity); (4) a specified relation (equation (8)) between their intensities must hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by resolving mutual pressures at contact points, introducing resultants (p,q,...) at centres and eliminating contact pressures to obtain the stated directional and intensity relations. The paper gives explicit ratio relations between resultants (e.g., sin-based ratios in the planes of adjacent centres).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications of Guldin (Pappus) rule to areas, volumes and centroid positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the rule of Pappus (Guldin's rule): the volume (or area) generated by revolving a plane figure about an external axis equals the area of the figure times the length of the path described by its centroid; example applications include finding volume of triangle revolution and locating the centroid of a triangle or parabola-based region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several illustrative problems are given: (1) triangle ABC revolved about base AC — relation between area, centroid path, and volume used to deduce centroid location; (2) paraboloid volume via revolution of area OPM. The rule is recommended for finding volumes and centroid positions, and examples show the algebraic manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horner — synthetic division / transformation principle for continuous approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: Synthetic division viewpoint: dividing a polynomial repeatedly by (x − r) yields successive remainders equal to the polynomial's coefficients in a transformed form; this leads to 'transformées' (mixed transforms) which alter form but preserve value/dimensions, and provides a practical basis for approximate root finding via recurring-series intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key axiom (Art. 9): 'Any quantity after being divided by a fraction whose numerator and denominator are equivalent, remains unaltered in its value.' Examples (Ex. I–III) illustrate operating with coefficients only, exchanging divisors for simple symbols to terminate division, and obtaining transformées. Corollaries include that absolute terms of transforms equal the result of substituting powers of r for a in the original, and practical memo (marginal memoranda) to track multipliers/indices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horner — general transformation algorithm and indexing/marginal-memoranda rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A general law for successive transformations: at each new transformation omit the first previously-employed multiplier, augment the rest by the new increment, retrograde them one step, and supply missing multipliers with the new increment; marginal memoranda list leading multipliers with decreasing indices to show how often to use each multiplier and where the increment was introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an operational rule (Art. 14) for carrying out multi-stage algebraic transformations (useful in synthetic division and mixed transformées). The memoranda are essential for practical bookkeeping when constructing successive transformed coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cockle — choice of transformed auxiliary equation to destroy consecutive terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking to eliminate m−2 consecutive terms of an equation (starting with the second), it is advantageous to assume a transformed equation in (v + p)^m (or similar) rather than v alone; this reduces the number and simplifies the remaining equations of condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method decreases number of conditions and simplifies algebra; applicable even when the terms to be destroyed are not consecutive or when modifying them in a prescribed way. The suggestion is a practical guideline for choosing an auxiliary substitution during algebraic transformation.
